segments.narration_text:
Everything that follows comes from the record — police and NSG timelines, court testimony, and the recordings themselves. And the record says this story doesn't start on November 26th. It starts five days earlier.

On the night of November 21st, ten men slipped out of Karachi aboard two cargo vessels, the Al Fauz and the Al Hussaini. For roughly thirty-eight hours, the Indian Navy never saw them. Each man carried an AK-47 and eight grenades. And dried fruit, for the journey.

On November 23rd, at around 4:30 PM, they seized an Indian fishing trawler, the MV Kuber. They killed four of its crew. The captain, they kept alive — to sail them to India. Within sight of Mumbai, they killed him too. No one was left who could warn anyone.

Except the warnings already existed. Indian intelligence had intercepted a satellite call on November 18th about a sea-borne attack. US intelligence had warned the Taj Hotels chairman, Ratan Tata, months before. Two warnings. Neither one changed what was waiting on the shore.

segments.narration_text:
They came ashore between 8:00 and 8:30 PM. Two landing points on Cuffe Parade: Macchimar Nagar and Badhwar Park. When curious locals asked who they were, they said they were students. Then they split into pairs.

Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus. One of the busiest railway stations on earth. Ajmal Kasab and his partner, Ismail Khan, walked into the passenger hall and opened fire. They threw grenades into the crowd. Fifty-eight people were killed here. It was the deadliest single site of the entire attack.

Leopold Café, a few minutes south. Two gunmen sprayed it with bullets and killed ten people. Then they fled on foot. The explosives they'd left in two taxis killed five more.

And at almost the same moment, pairs of gunmen walked into the Taj Mahal Palace and the Oberoi-Trident. Two five-star hotels that would become the main stage for three days. The fifth target was one most of the world had never heard of: a small Jewish outreach centre called Nariman House.

Five locations. Ten minutes. Ten men. This is what eighteen months of rehearsal looks like — the curriculum from our last file, finally deployed. But rehearsal alone doesn't explain what happened next.

From CST, Kasab and Ismail Khan moved on foot to Cama Hospital. It was around 10:30 PM. The staff saw them coming. They locked patients into their rooms. That decision likely saved lives.

Outside, three of Mumbai's most senior officers tried to stop them from a jeep: Anti-Terrorism Squad chief Hemant Karkare, additional commissioner Ashok Kamte, and senior inspector Vijay Salaskar. All three were killed. The gunmen took the same police jeep and drove off. They didn't get far. Near Girgaum Chowpatty, officers from the Gamdevi police station stopped the jeep. Ismail Khan was killed. Kasab, wounded, was taken alive.

He was the only one of the ten who would be. And that one survivor is the reason the world would later hear, in his own words, how the operation was built. By 1:00 AM, this thread of the night was over. The other four were just getting started.

On the morning of the 27th came a decision that has been criticised ever since. Local police were told to stand down and hand full authority to the National Security Guard — India's federal counter-terrorism force. Its commandos had to fly in from Delhi. The city waited.

At the Taj, NSG commandos were inside by around 7:20 that evening. Until then, the fighting came in bursts: small evacuations, sudden gunfire, a fire on the fourth floor.

At the Oberoi-Trident, the NSG arrived around 5:30 PM. A naval helicopter surveyed the building from above. Roughly 250 guests would be brought out of this hotel alone, in waves through the night.

At Nariman House, there was nothing to negotiate. Two gunmen held the rabbi, his wife, and several others. The NSG would not move in until the following morning.

By the end of the second day, none of the three sieges was over. Twenty-four hours, and no end in sight.

segments.narration_text:
The 28th is when two of the sieges finally end. Neither ends the way anyone hoped.

At Nariman House, just after 7:30 in the morning, NSG commandos fast-roped from helicopters onto the roof, with snipers covering them from nearby buildings. It took most of the day. By 7:30 in the evening, they had found all six hostages — the rabbi and his wife among them — murdered by their captors. An hour later, both gunmen were dead, and the siege was declared over.

At the Oberoi-Trident, the operation ended around 3:00 PM. Officials counted one hundred and forty-three hostages rescued alive. Twenty-four bodies were recovered. Both terrorists inside were killed.

The Taj, though, was still burning. Six more bodies were recovered that afternoon, followed by ten grenade blasts between 2:53 and 3:59 PM. By evening, officials believed only one gunman was left inside. They were wrong.

segments.narration_text:
In the early hours of the 29th, the Taj shook again. Five explosions, between 3:40 and 4:10 AM. Ten minutes later, officials declared the hotel under government control. By 5:05, they had taken it back.

At 7:30 AM, fire was still burning on the first floor. Black smoke rose from the second. Witnesses described a gun battle still under way. Then, sometime between 8:00 and 8:50 AM — accounts differ by minutes — commandos declared the hotel finally, fully secured. The NSG called it Operation Tornado.

From the first shots at CST to the last all-clear at the Taj, the siege had run just under sixty hours.

segments.narration_text:
By the official count, 166 people were killed. More than a dozen of them were security personnel, and at least 26 were foreign nationals. More than 300 were injured. Nine of the ten attackers died. Only Ajmal Kasab survived — tried, convicted, and executed in 2012.

On 12 February 2009, Pakistan's government admitted something for the first time. The attack had been planned and launched, at least in part, from Pakistani soil. It continued to deny any official state involvement. It denied, specifically, any role for its intelligence services — a role multiple foreign investigators have alleged.

The city didn't wait for answers. CST was running again within hours. Leopold Café was reportedly serving customers within four days. The Taj reopened to guests within about a month.
